quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Description, Averages, and Rates
quizzes.intro: Check foundational descriptive ideas before sampling, causation, and charts.

questions.prompt: What should come before calculating statistics?

options.text: A clear question, unit of observation, and decision the answer should support
A chart with no labels
A causal claim with no data
Deleting inconvenient points immediately

questions.explanation: Bad questions produce elegant nonsense; clarify first.

wrongExplanations.d: Outliers need investigation, not reflex deletion.

questions.prompt: When is the median often more useful than the mean?

options.text: Never; means always represent “typical” best
When data are skewed or extreme values pull the mean
Only for categorical colors like red/blue averages
Only when you want to hide variation

questions.explanation: Medians resist outlier pull and often better match “typical” for skewed data.

wrongExplanations.c: Category labels are not averaged that way.

options.text: Two datasets can share a mean yet feel very different in reliability
Spread is irrelevant if an average exists
Only the maximum value ever matters
Variation proves causation

questions.explanation: Center without spread hides unpredictability and risk.

wrongExplanations.c: Extremes are not the whole story.
wrongExplanations.d: Variation is descriptive, not causal proof.

questions.prompt: What question should you ask of every percentage?

options.text: “Percent of what?” (what is the base?)
“Can we remove the denominator?”
“How do we make it sound bigger?”
“Can we skip units?”

questions.explanation: Percentages mislead when bases differ or are hidden.

questions.prompt: Why can raw counts mislead compared with rates?

options.text: Because exposure/denominators differ—e.g., returns should be per sale
Because rates are never useful
Because counting is unethical
Because bigger counts always mean better quality

questions.explanation: Rates account for opportunity or volume; raw counts ignore exposure.

wrongExplanations.b: Rates are often the operational truth.
wrongExplanations.d: Volume can inflate counts without worse rates.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Samples, Probability, and Causation
quizzes.intro: Test sampling intuition, uncertainty language, and correlation vs causation.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between sample and population?

options.text: A sample is the subset measured; a population is the full group of interest
They are identical by definition always
Populations are always smaller than samples
Samples remove all uncertainty automatically

questions.explanation: Inference uses samples to learn about populations—with uncertainty.

wrongExplanations.b: They differ unless you measured everyone.

questions.prompt: What does a huge biased sample do?

options.text: Fix bias through size alone
Remain biased—sometimes more confidently wrong
Guarantee causation
Eliminate the need for definitions

questions.explanation: Size reduces random noise but does not cure systematic bias.

wrongExplanations.a: Bias is not fixed by N alone.
wrongExplanations.c: Design, not size alone, supports causal claims.

questions.prompt: What is the key warning about correlation?

options.text: Correlation always proves causation
Variables can move together without one causing the other
Correlation is meaningless in all cases
Only ice cream studies matter

questions.explanation: Association is not enough for cause; experiments and careful designs help.

wrongExplanations.c: Correlations can still be useful clues.
wrongExplanations.d: The ice cream example is illustrative, not exclusive.

questions.prompt: What helps A/B tests estimate causal effects?

options.text: Random assignment to variants with predefined metrics and enough data
Peeking once and declaring victory after an afternoon wiggle
Changing many things with no metric plan
Using only anecdotes from one power user

questions.explanation: Randomization plus disciplined metrics supports causal inference.

wrongExplanations.b: Early peeking and noise chasing mislead.
wrongExplanations.d: Anecdotes inform mechanism, not alone causal proof.

questions.prompt: What should you look for with poll or estimate headlines?

options.text: Only the single point number
Uncertainty cues such as margin of error plus sample details
Whether the chart is 3D enough
Whether jargon intimidates questions away

questions.explanation: Point estimates without uncertainty feel falsely precise.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Charts, Ethics, and Careful Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on visualization honesty, metric definitions, and professional numeracy.

options.text: Check axes, units, time range, and what is missing
Trust truncated axes without question
Prefer pie charts with dozens of slices always
Ignore dual-axis distortions

questions.explanation: Axes and context determine whether a chart informs or manipulates.

wrongExplanations.d: Dual axes often mislead when unexplained.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between percentage points and percent change?

options.text: There is no difference
A move from 10% to 12% is +2 percentage points and +20% relative
Percentage points are only for temperature
Relative percent change ignores the starting value

questions.explanation: Confusing points with relative percent causes bad decisions.

wrongExplanations.a: They differ and both should be named carefully.
wrongExplanations.d: Relative change depends on the baseline.

options.text: Ambiguous definitions create fake debates and garbage analysis
Definitions slow teams down with no benefit
“Engagement” is self-explanatory worldwide
Software removes the need for meaning

questions.explanation: Operational definitions make numbers comparable and discussable.

wrongExplanations.d: Tools do not replace judgment or definitions.

questions.prompt: What is an ethical statistics communication practice?

options.text: Cherry-pick windows that flatter a story
Disclose uncertainty and limits; do not use jargon to shut down questions
Hide denominators
Present noise wiggles as destinies

questions.explanation: Honest communication includes context and humility.

questions.prompt: How should AI be used with statistics?

options.text: As an unchecked source of methods and certainty
As a helper for summaries/plots while humans verify assumptions and critical claims
To invent sample sizes
To replace asking “compared to what?”

questions.explanation: Accountability for claims stays with you.

questions.prompt: Which habit best captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: When you see a number, ask: Compared to what? Says who (sample)? What’s the spread or uncertainty?
Treat every dashboard wiggle as a crisis narrative
Equate correlation with proven cause
Trust naked numbers without definitions

questions.explanation: Those three questions operationalize beginner statistical literacy.
